item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] ​​​​Morocco: Ten years after the Rif uprising, its leaders are still jailed and its demands unmet
item.description:
​​​​Morocco: Ten years after the Rif uprising, its leaders are still jailed and its demands unmet

Submitted by Renee Boskaljon on Wed, 10/28/2026 - 08:01
A decade after fishmonger Mouhcine Fikri’s death triggered widespread protests, economic hardship and repression persist across the marginalised region
Moroccans take part in a candlelight vigil in Casablanca on 8 August 2017 for a protestor who died in the Rif protests in northern Morocco after he was hit in the head during clashes with security forces (Stringer/AFP)
Off

“Our family has been through a lot. My mother’s health has deteriorated, but despite everything, she continues to hold on.”

Mohamed Ahamjik has done everything he can to help his family since his younger brother, Nabil, was arrested in 2017 over his role in Morocco’s Rif protest movement. He is serving a 20-year prison sentence.

Since then, Mohamed has worked to raise awareness about his case.

“This has always been a duty towards my mother, my brother Nabil and our family,” he told Middle East Eye, speaking ahead of Wednesday’s anniversary marking a decade since protests erupted in the kingdom’s northern Rif mountains over poverty, marginalisation and underdevelopment.

The movement was sparked by the death of fishmonger Mouhcine Fikri, who was crushed inside a rubbish truck in Al Hoceima on 28 October 2016 while trying to retrieve his confiscated catch.

Ten years on, the wounds left by repression and decades of marginalisation are still felt across the region, while six prominent Hirak figures remain in prison, including the movement's leader Nasser Zefzafi, who was sentenced to 20 years.

According to Moroccan historian Maati Monjib, the Rif uprising was “one of the most significant social movements” in Morocco since King Mohammed VI ascended the throne in 1999.

Initially centered in Al Hoceima and its surrounding province, the protests were tolerated for several months before authorities launched a crackdown in late May, resulting in hundreds of arrests.

Authorities branded the movement as separatist - a label Monjib described as “false accusations made to discredit their demands”. He told MEE that although a small minority of activists expressed separatist views, mostly in Facebook groups, the main leaders who remain imprisoned never did.

The state’s response reached a new turning point on 20 July, when riot police used tear gas and batons to disperse demonstrators in Al Hoceima, severely injuring 22‑year‑old Imad el‑Attabi, who died the following month.

The crackdown triggered widespread solidarity protests across Morocco throughout the summer of 2017.

An uprising against ‘hogra’

Nabil played an important role in the movement. His activism, Mohamed told MEE, was driven by his rejection of “hogra”, a term referring to humiliation and oppression, and by what he saw as “the historical injustice that the region suffered for decades from the central power”.

His arrest did not come as a surprise to his family.

“After the parliamentary majority falsely accused the Rif movement of separatism, we understood that a vast wave of arrests was being prepared,” Mohamed said.

‘After the parliamentary majority falsely accused the Rif movement of separatism, we understood that a vast wave of arrests was being prepared’

- Mohamed Ahamjik, brother of a jailed Rif activist

Transferred between several prisons over the years, Nabil is now held in Tangier.

From his cell, he wrote a master’s thesis on the Rif’s relationship with the state at Mohammed I University in Oujda, earning an 18 out of 20 and a recommendation for publication. Now a doctoral student, he staged a 10‑day hunger strike last month after authorities denied him a proper space to work on his PhD.

In recent years, rights groups have denounced the arrests of Rif protesters, along with allegations of torture, ill-treatment in custody and violations of fair-trial standards.

The crackdown did not stop with those who took to the streets. Journalists who covered the protests and activists living abroad were also caught up in the wave of repression.

Said El Amrani, a digital creator, former journalist and human rights activist, is one of them. Born in the Rif, he moved to Belgium in the 1990s to pursue his studies. In 1991, he was briefly arrested upon his arrival at Tangier airport for his activism.

In 2016, two months before the outbreak of the Rif protests, he returned to the region for what would be the last time. As the crackdown extended to the diaspora, he and other activists have not returned since.

“Since the beginning of the Rif movement, at least 11 activists have been arrested when arriving in Morocco. Two of them were sentenced to prison, one of them is still in jail,” El Amrani told MEE, adding that like many other activists in the diaspora, he has also been targeted online.

“Photos were taken from my personal social media account, including pictures of my younger daughter, manipulated to create sexualised images, and then shared on Facebook.” He has also been repeatedly targeted by a news outlet reportedly close to Morocco’s intelligence services.

Today, he told MEE, the region remains under tight security. “They built at least five new police stations since the protests,” he said.

A history of revolt and repression

Over the past century, the history of the Rif has been marked by resistance and repression.

Jamal El Khattabi, born in Al Hoceima in the early 1960s, grew up on stories of armed struggle and of relatives killed in the Rif War, the anti‑colonial uprising fought from 1921 to 1926 between Berber tribes of the Rif and Spanish - later French - colonial forces.

His father was among the young fighters who joined Abdelkrim El Khattabi, the leader of the resistance movement who united the Rif’s tribes and proclaimed an independent republic in 1921.

It took the combined forces of France and Spain to crush the uprising in 1926, marking the end of the self-proclaimed republic.

On his mother’s side, El Khattabi’s grandfather died before she was born. The family was told he had suffocated after exposure to chemical weapons used by the Spanish to squash the resistance.

The repression did not end with his parents’ generation. After Morocco gained independence from French and Spanish colonial rule in 1956, the army under Crown Prince Hassan, later King Hassan II, brutally suppressed uprisings in several regions, including the Rif.

Jamal, who joined activist groups during university, was arrested twice under Hassan II, who was known for ruling with an iron fist.

After his first arrest in 1989, he was beaten with a thick stick and thrown from a roof, leaving him with a serious back injury. He described being taken blindfolded to Derb Moulay Cherif in Casablanca, where the torture included severe beatings, threats involving dogs and prolonged exposure to bright lights.

“I could no longer stand without them having to ‘help’ me,” he told MEE. After his second detention, he fled Morocco for Spain and eventually settled in the Netherlands.

When Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999 after his father’s death, the kingdom appeared to be entering a more open era, with promises of reform, and the years of political persecution, torture and enforced disappearances seemed to be over.

The Arab Spring protests of 2011 led to constitutional changes that formally limited the monarchy’s powers, but hopes for lasting political reform soon began to fade.

Repression intensified in the years that followed, becoming particularly pronounced after the Rif protests. Over the past decade, numerous reports have shown how the monarchy crushes dissent, increasingly relying on surveillance technologies - including the Israeli spyware Pegasus - as well as defamation campaigns and unfair trials.

The worsening crackdown was stark during last year’s Gen Z protests over failing public services, unemployment and corruption, even as billions were poured into stadiums for the 2030 World Cup.

While the Rif protests were initially tolerated for months, the Gen Z demonstrations were crushed within weeks: 6,000 people were arrested, most of them in the first days.

A year later, around 700 remain in jail, including dozens of minors, according to the Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH).

‘They have no future’

The memory of the Rif uprising a decade ago has taken on new relevance amid a turbulent year for Morocco.

While the kingdom has experienced rapid economic growth and made history last month with the election of its first female prime minister, deep economic and social frustrations remain. Youth unemployment, at 37 percent, and rising living costs are among the deepest issues.

Those frustrations came into sharp focus again this summer, when tens of thousands of people attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Many of them were young Moroccans from the Rif region.

‘There continues to be a deep desire for dignity and equal recognition - where a Moroccan, in the Rif or elsewhere, should be the equal of every other Moroccan, regardless of status or background’

- Maati Monjib, historian

While Atlantic cities such as Casablanca, Rabat and Tangier, and tourist hotspots like Marrakech, have drawn billions in investment and gleaming new infrastructure, the Rif and other impoverished regions like the Atlas Mountains have been left on the margins.

The Rif has the highest number of cancer patients in Morocco, a toll linked to the chemical bombs Spain dropped during the Rif War. Yet the hospitals and specialised equipment that could treat patients lie hours away.

This mirrors a wider divide, one that shaped the debate in the recent elections: a Morocco of two speeds. In Tangier, the Tanger Med port, industrial zones, car factories and booming exports drive rapid growth. In the Rif, young people still face high unemployment and few prospects.

The state did respond to some of the protesters’ demands: a new faculty affiliated with the University of Tetouan was opened. But in El Amrani’s view, most initiatives fall short. A hospital was recently built, “but there is not enough medical staff”.

For young people, “there is no work,” he added. “Many have left, most of them clandestinely for Europe. Others have moved to Moroccan cities such as Tangier and Tetouan.”

For decades, thousands of families in the borderlands lived off the informal trade that flowed through the Spanish autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla. In recent years, as controls on the borders with the Spanish enclaves tightened, that trade became impossible.

That left the borderlands poorer and pushed more and more young people to risk their lives to reach Europe, as the latest mass attempt to cross to Ceuta this summer showed.

“They have nothing to lose,” El Amrani said. Many are out of school, without work and without access to healthcare. “They feel they have no future. For them, the only solution is to leave.”

Monjib, who himself spent three months in prison for his activism and is now routinely targeted by the authorities, told MEE that although heavy state repression largely paralysed the Rif movement and shifted its focus toward demanding the release of political prisoners, its core pursuit of equality endures.

“There continues to be a deep desire for dignity and equal recognition - where a Moroccan, in the Rif or elsewhere, should be the equal of every other Moroccan, regardless of status or background,” he said.

Inside Morocco

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How UK antisemitism report could worsen the very problem it warns against
item.description:
How UK antisemitism report could worsen the very problem it warns against

Submitted by Gary Spedding on Tue, 10/27/2026 - 15:37
The government risks teaching Jewish pupils that support for Israel is integral to their identity, and that Palestine solidarity is inherently threatening
UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell speaks in Liverpool on 27 September 2026 (Darren Staples/AFP)
Off

Last week, Education Secretary Lucy Powell accepted Sir David Bell’s review into antisemitism in British schools and colleges.

While billed as “independent”, however, this does not appear to be a neutral examination of prejudice against Jewish pupils. Rather, it is a document shaped by what I perceive to be undeclared ties between UK and Israeli educational and advocacy networks, an undue emphasis on Palestine solidarity as intimidatory and problematic, and a near-exclusive reliance on the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)’s working definition of antisemitism. The definition’s appended examples disproportionately target and chill speech about Israel.

The review found that almost three in five Jewish students between the ages of 16 and 19 reported that they had experienced or witnessed antisemitism, rising from about one in five overall. This is an alarming statistic. 

Yet the study itself notes that the claim rests on a “low sample size of 92 students who identify as Jewish” within a survey of more than 5,000 people. The data simply does not justify the findings.

By treating antisemitism as a form of racism requiring politicised safeguarding and wider adoption of the IHRA definition, the review risks weaponising antisemitism against Palestine solidarity in education. Further, by addressing antisemitism in isolation from broader conversations about racism, and by restricting support for Palestine, Britain risks alienating students and worsening antisemitism in our schools.

Bell’s appointment as an “independent” reviewer sits uneasily with his background. He previously served as permanent secretary at the Department for Education and chief inspector of schools in England. 

He is listed as having sat on the National Council of the Academic Study Group on Israel and the Middle East, whose mission is to “initiate or expand active links and research collaboration between academics, specialists and centres-of-excellence in the UK and their counterparts in Israel”. Its director, John Levy, has longstanding ties to the Friends of Israel Educational Foundation and Academic Friends of Israel.

These connections should have prompted the Department for Education to question Bell’s impartiality - yet none of this appears to have been formally declared as a conflict of interest. It is also notable that, in 2005, Bell was accused of Islamophobia while head of Ofsted, after he said that Muslim schools risked undermining social cohesion.

Criticism reframed

Based on my own extensive research, I believe the composition of the review’s reference group raises further concerns about impartiality and neutrality, as the organisational links of some members highlight a substantial, institutionalised ecosystem shaping what many Jewish pupils encounter on Israel and Jewish identity. 

These are not abstract associations, yet they receive next to no scrutiny. Israel advocacy organisations, and educational charities with explicit pro-Israel missions, deliver talks, workshops, resources, and engagement programmes to thousands of students nationwide.

Such programmes explicitly seek to cultivate emotional attachment, associate Jewish identity with support for Israel, and encourage Jewish pupils to actively advocate for the country.

Attempts to reframe as antisemitic any criticism of Israel or solidarity with Palestinians, places Jewish pupils at the forefront of a fraught battle they largely did not choose. Such discourse frames Jewish identity as requiring support for Israel, while Palestine solidarity is cast as a hostile, existential threat.

If the government restricts Palestine solidarity in schools by using antisemitism as a convenient scapegoat, the backlash could have dire consequences

The exploitation of legitimate fears and vulnerabilities, whereby young Jews are encouraged to feel intimidated by expressions of support for Palestinian rights, has been examined in documentaries such as Israelism.

The access that Israel advocacy organisations have to schools should raise serious concerns about neutrality in the opposite direction, particularly given their potential to promote negative tropes and stereotypes about Palestine and Palestinians.

In a similar vein, one of the review’s most alarming outputs is its reinforcement of the notion that Palestine solidarity is inherently linked to antisemitism. This polarisation of discussion around the UK’s genuine antisemitism problem is dangerous. Many leftists, who should be natural allies of oppressed minorities, are so fed up with having Palestine solidarity denounced as antisemitic that they shut down when it comes to tackling actual antisemitism.

If the government restricts Palestine solidarity in schools by using antisemitism as a convenient scapegoat, the backlash could have dire consequences, not least for Jewish students facing genuine antisemitism. This could hamper efforts to implement a coherent strategy.

Indeed, efforts to combat antisemitism are far more successful when bigotry is tackled through intersectional approaches that allow every student to feel seen, while simultaneously learning about the specific, devastating and lethal history of anti-Jewish oppression. Educators can highlight Jewish historical trauma not to minimise others’ experiences, but to build deep, empathetic connections across cultural and ethnic boundaries.

Middle East Eye reached out to Bell and the Department for Education for comment, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. 

Political pressure

I would go so far as to warn that political pressure seeking to exploit antisemitism to shield Israel from criticism, threatens to strip away the infrastructure needed to combat it. This further undermines meaningful efforts to tackle hatred of Jews.

When allegations of antisemitism are weaponised to excuse Israel’s crimes, a question mark is placed over those reporting it, in a way that victims of other forms of racism do not face. When a Jewish person reports experiencing antisemitism today, observers might wonder: was this actual antisemitism, or have they been taught to view Palestine solidarity and anti-Zionism as anti-Jewish hatred and a personal attack?

This chilling effect, already felt in free speech and the exploration of Palestine-related issues, also threatens the fight against antisemitism. It risks encouraging dismissive attitudes towards anti-Jewish prejudice, hatred and oppression.

Let’s be crystal clear: antisemitism is real, pervasive, cyclical and pernicious. Jews should not have to fight this blight alone, and Jewish children must be protected as an absolute priority. We can acknowledge that antisemitism is a growing problem in our schools and society, while guarding against its weaponisation in the context of Palestine solidarity.

Antisemitism reviewer David Bell said Muslim schools could threaten UK's 'coherence'
Read More »

In 2024, the Institute for Jewish Policy Research found that 23 percent of parents reported their child had experienced antisemitism directly at school, in the vicinity of school, or travelling to or from school. This is not insignificant, but it is far below the figures published in the Bell review.

The review’s framing worryingly subordinates classic antisemitic abuse - Hitler salutes, Holocaust jokes, money stereotypes, physical assaults, isolation and intimidation - to concerns about Palestine solidarity badges, flags, symbols and “political expression”.

An analysis by Newscord, examining the review’s text, found that roughly a quarter of it concerns Israel, Palestine or political expression. The terms of reference effectively locked in the IHRA approach from the outset, precluding consideration of alternative definitions that do not focus so heavily on criticism of Israel. Many responses to the call for evidence, including 158 critical of the review itself or of the use of the IHRA definition, were not meaningfully reflected or quoted.

In addition, despite the review identifying “confusion around the boundary between legitimate political expression and antisemitism”, a majority of those directly asked - 526 out of 590 - said they could distinguish between the two. This finding was omitted from the main report.

The government risks teaching Jewish pupils that support for Israel is integral to their identity, and that Palestine solidarity, or criticism of Israeli policy, is inherently threatening to them as Jews. It also risks teaching non-Jewish students that their Jewish classmates see Israel as integral to their identity, and that suggesting otherwise is deeply racist. 

This reinforces, rather than challenges, the harmful assumption that Jewish students must “support or have views on the state of Israel” because of their Jewish identity - ironically, something the report itself confirms causes deep discomfort among Jewish pupils and staff.

John Healey found time to hold a meeting with Martin Lewis, the founder of MoneySavingExpert.com, in Downing Street this morning. Lewis is one of the most trusted voices on personal finance in Britain, and he has been campaigning for standing charges to be removed from gas bills for some time.

Speaking to the media afterwards, Lewis said Healey was in a good mood. He said he asked the chancellor if there would be a support scheme to help people with energy bills from January, when costs are set to rise sharply. Lewis said Healey would not confirm anything, but he said that “reading between the lines” he gathered that there will be an announcement on this. Lewis speculated that this could be an increase in the warm homes discount, or it could be help for people in lower council tax bands.

The biggest issue in energy right now is that we’re expecting a 27% rise in the price cap in January. I asked the Chancellor whether he will be intervening on that. He told me I’d have to wait for the budget, but reading between the lines, yes, there will be an announcement today.
